question:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 2-month history of intermittent right lower abdominal
pain that increases after prolonged sitting. She denies any recent trauma but mentions that she has
been doing more core-strengthening exercises lately. Vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal
examination shows no abnormalities. Musculoskeletal examination reveals a tender point at one-third
of the distance between the anterior superior iliac spine and the midline. She rates the pain as a 6 on a
scale of 0 to 10; the pain does not radiate. The patient consents to treatment with counterstrain. The
most appropriate positioning to treat this patient is Answer Choices: (A) supine with the hip extended
and externally rotated (B) supine with the hip flexed, adducted, and internally rotated (C) prone with
bilateral hip flexion and abduction (D) prone with the hip flexed and internally rotated (E) supine with
bilateral hip flexion and neutral rotation (F) supine with the hip flexed and externally rotated (G) prone
with the hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated (H) side-lying with the hip extended and internally
rotated (I) side-lying with the hip flexed and adducted (J) prone with the hip extended and internally
rotated
 A. side-lying with the hip flexed and adducted
B. supine with the hip flexed, adducted, and internally rotated
C. prone with the hip extended and internally rotated
D. prone with the hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated
E. supine with the hip extended and externally rotated
F. supine with the hip flexed and externally rotated
G. supine with bilateral hip flexion and neutral rotation
H. prone with the hip flexed and internally rotated
I. prone with bilateral hip flexion and abduction
J. side-lying with the hip extended and internally rotated
